segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We are going to talk for a little while.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m thankful, too, like you said a while ago, this morning we have seen another day of sunshine.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s because our God is so kind we are here today.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s the way it is. We are not promised tomorrow.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, no, no.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Every day, that’s it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re not promised tomorrow.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: No, we’re not. No, we’re not.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We might not be alive later on.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Let’s say when I’m going home, I could get hit or have a heart attack or something. Or something else might happen. We’re not promised tomorrow. That’s the way it is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK, what’s your name in English?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Levi is my name in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Levi.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Owl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Owl, yeah. Now what do they call you in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Dvyulisini.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dvyugsesd.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Dvyulisini.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dvlisini.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: When I was born, it was getting dark and that’s why they gave me that name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, yeah.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Dvyulisini Uguku.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born, when you came into this world?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I came from Greasy. I grew up in Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you were born there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Around Greasy, but I was born here in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, here in Tahlequah. Do you still go to Beaver church?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yes, Beaver is what they call it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you still go to church there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, I still go there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh there.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: When I’m not sick, I go there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The one guy I used to pastor with went there for a while his name was Jess Glass he was helping them for a while at Beaver.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: People from this way were helping us out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They come from that way. Rusty was the name of one. He was a real good preacher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was also a good singer.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I agree. I agree.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about where you grew up?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s the only place I grew up, around Greasy. A little over 30 years I was around Greasy. I’m living in Stilwell now, in town, closer to the hospital and grocery stores.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. So, when you were a little boy, you were growing up there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, Greasy. We always had a farm. My dad used to work and raise peaches and blackberries, strawberries, and beans. Then it was all peaches. That’s where I started. When I was little, I would be working just like the men. That’s when I grew up when I did that, and then they sold it. And then I went to Stilwell at Auffet’s farm and started there, and I was watching peaches, apples, and different things there. I really did like it. I was riding on a tractor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were really used to that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, I was really used to that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were experienced in doing that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s why that boss called me over there. He was part owner at Greasy and when they sold it, I started at the chicken plant for a little while. And when that boss found out I was working there, he came over there and asked me if I would come back and help him, he said. Immediately I said yes because I liked working outside. It was a really big farm. It took a week to cut the grass. I started early in the morning till dark and when that was done, on Monday, I would start spraying apples and different things all week. And when that was done, the grass had already grown again and then again. Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about when...you said Greasy and Stilwell. When you got married, would you just say you lived there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: When I got married at Greasy. Did you know Barry Wayne Christie?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Barry Wayne Christie...

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: From Marble. He came from Marble City. He was really a good preacher. He married us the first time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So where did you mostly live? Or where did you say you lived now? So you said you live in Stilwell now?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I live in Stilwell now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you’ve probably lived there a long time.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, probably for over 20 years, going on 30. I’m 68 years old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You are just a young man.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I’m a young man. I was telling them, that girl will say, “Haw, Papa.”

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Like I said, at Greasy it was really good growing up. You could walk around on the road in the middle of night, and nobody would bother you. Sometimes you would meet somebody, and nobody started anything. We would talk, and they would go on and I would go up the hill. And sometimes them Johnson boys, they lived down the hill. Me and my brother would go down the hill on weekends. We would play all day, horseshoes or play ball. We would leave around midnight, and we would walk through the woods and come to the top of the hill at the peach orchard, and we would go down the hill. Sometimes we would see something walking. I would be doing this... and my brother would say, “Don’t run!” My dad used to say, "Don’t ever run.” I would have salt. He said, "Throw the salt behind you as you’re walking.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did it really stop when you threw the salt?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, it did stop. I never asked the reason. And sometimes we would walk on the road and at a certain place, something would appear, and it would walk in the woods beside us. We could hear its footsteps, but we kept walking. My brother would say, “Don’t run.” I would say, “OK.” We kept walking and talking and it was still walking. It would follow us for a long ways, then it would stop and we would turn toward our house. There was something living there a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Something could’ve been watching y’all while you were walking.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: And when we would go to church, we walked – we didn’t have a car – a little in the woods and then on the road and then in the woods and back on the road. And we came out below the church. There was something there, too. It would also walk beside us. My dad was very brave. I was scared. He always had a knife. He would say, “Keep walking,” and he would go after it. It would back away all the time. It would take him further and when he would come back, it would come back. And it would turn back and then after a while a mom would say, “You come back!” He would come back. As we would get back to our turn off, where the cows crossed, what’s called the cattle guard, there was something there, too. It would be standing there. It stood about this high; it was doing this as it would stand in front of us. He would pull his knife out again. He would tell it to come here, but it would back away from him. He told us when it backs up to cross. He would follow it with his knife. He would stand on this side and when it did that, we would cross there. Really was something there. I don’t know what it was. We grew up there and it was really good. And it was funny, I wasn’t scared of anything after a while. “It won’t do anything to you,” Dad said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what I was told one time. It won’t do anything to you. You are going to hurt yourself if you run. That’s what they used to tell us.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: You are going to kill yourself if you run, they used to say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they used to tell us, but sometimes it was scary. You had to run.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: You really did, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Things were really strange back then.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, ain’t it? Like I said, there were a lot of things. It wasn’t like it is nowadays. Sometimes drunks would be walking and whooping. It was mostly my uncles from around Greasy. They would come up the hill. They would be coming from somewhere whooping. They never bothered anybody. They would just go home.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One of my grandmothers lived kinda on the ridge. Sometime, long time ago, they were bingo players. They would have bananas and apples for prizes. Sometimes there would be somebody hollering down the road. They would be hollering as they passed by. They would say, “There is that drunkard.”

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: People knew who they were by the whooping or something. They knew who it was. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about... Can you tell me about the places that you worked? You didn’t do anything else?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That was the only thing I had started – the peach orchard. And then, like I said, the last time I started, the boss, the real boss’ dad passed away. And then the boy took over that, but he didn’t know how because his dad was really smart. For a few years that boy did really good but he was listening to the other boy that worked there. He was buying too much Christmas stuff. We had a lot and schools were coming there to get some and that other boy said, “Let’s raise cattle. There is money in that.” And he listened to him and they started to get behind on bills borrowing money and he used up all the money he had he borrowed from his mom. No, it was the money his dad left him, which he used all of it to pay it back. And he borrowed from his mom again. That’s when I realized it was gonna close down. “Boy, I need for you to help me ‘cause I always wanted to go out of state and work like Texas,” one time I was laying there, and I prayed. It was like He heard me and the wind hit me like He answered me. The very next day, a boy came and asked me if I would help him. “I don’t know how to do stuff like that,” I told him. “But you can learn,” he said. I said, “Yeah, I’ll try to learn.” “Be ready on Monday,” he said. “Where are we going?” I said. “To Texas. Dallas first,” he said, “and then San Antonio and then Houston.” That’s when I started and I worked for four years. We were fixing and building stores. That was really good. The money was good, but it was taking me away from my family too much. About that time I got sick. I think we were in Kentucky or West Virginia. They gave me my own boys now I knew a lot. I took them and we were waiting on the machine, the scissor lift, to climb on and it wasn’t getting there, so we used two scaffolds. We put them pretty high. I told them boys, “Let’s paint as far as we can reach.” And they said, “OK.” And I went that way. They said, “You’re the boss.” I said, “No, I can’t be.” Still I have to be doing something. I climbed up sideways. And when I got to the top of the platform, my legs got numb. I hit my knees and I fell off. I fell on some stuff they had laying. There I hit hard, here. I couldn’t hardly do anything after that. I did that for a little over four years, that. But now I have trouble with my breathing. It interfered with my lungs. And then I applied for help, but it’s not worth it. It’s not fixed income, it’s not enough money to pay anything, but it was all I could do. I’m getting crippled and my back and like we said, I’m thankful that God watches over me. Yes, sir.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He provides things when we need it.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That place they have wood in Stilwell, I help them sometimes. I was helping them for a little while. That boss was paying cash. But I couldn’t do it, so I told them, “I quit that. I’m not able to do it.” Just two days went by they were calling me on the phone asking where I was at. I told them, “I’m home.” I have quit three times there, ‘cause sometimes Cherokee elders come in there. I translate for them if they want something and I also help them. That’s what they like, because those Cherokees can’t talk good and I translate for them and that’s what the boss likes. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I used to work at the clinic in Jay.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Jay, there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, when the Cherokee and the doctors didn’t understand each other, they would come get me and then I would go that way. That’s what I used to do was translate so they could understand. I would translate. But now there are very few living like that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, there really is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about... How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Five: two boys and three girls.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they are all grown up now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, they are grown up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All of them.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s what I thought, “When they grow up.” Then I thought I was going to get some good rest, but I didn’t and now it’s my grandkids it’s as if they were my own I watch them the one girl that born last is 30 years old she used to stay with me all the time when I separated with her mom she didn’t want her mom she came with me and I was working at the orchard. I got a little travel trailer. She stayed with me there. She was cleaning and she was just a little girl. I would take her to school in the mornings, and her mom would get her in the evenings. And when I got off work in the evening, I would go get her and we would come back. I have seven grandkids and one great.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They all have girls and no boys.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They are going to order you around when they grow up.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I told them, “Maybe you’re pretty smart that you don’t have any children.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your siblings? How many are there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I have one brother. That’s the only one I have. He is really crippled. He is... what do they call them? Diabetic.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, sugar diabetes.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: He has it bad. He can fall down fast and I watch out for him. I have two sisters. One still lives out towards Greasy, and one lives close by. When she was a little girl, just a few months, her mom didn’t want her. She was cross-eyed and there was something wrong with her leg. She was kind of crippled and her mom didn’t want her. My dad said, “I am going to take her in,” and him and Mom fixed papers. We went and got that girl. But now she has grown up she is 46 years old. She really has gotten better. Her eyes have gotten better. They were taking her to the doctor in Oklahoma City, and she had surgery on her leg. She walks real good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now she is doing good.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Now she is doing good. Nowadays her real mom will say, “Hi, my daughter.” She said, “No, Mom is dead,” she told them the other day, “And my dad is dead, too. You’re not my mom,” she told her. “You gave me up when I was little,” she told her, “And they raised me, and the only one I got left is Levi. I think of him a lot. He is just like my dad,” she told that woman. She lives nearby and I really watch her, too, and I go check on my brother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did her mother think when she told her that?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: She just got quiet. She didn’t seem to like it. She just turned around and went the other way. She grew up, I watch her real good all the time. If she wants something, she will be saying, “Bub,” on the phone. And I will say, “What is it?” She will be wanting to go to the store. “Can I go get something to eat?” I’ll say, “OK, I’ll be there in a little bit,” and I go get her. Yeah, they are the only ones left now. And my uncles, there is only one left now: Daniel Otechi, we call him, and my aunt is Lucille. They are the only ones at Beaver Church. They got it going. I don’t know what is going to happen there when Lucille passes away at that church. That’s what I tell people, that we need to learn and keep going the way elders have taught us. We should be the same and keep going.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, let the love continue to keep it going.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes when an elder passes away, things can stop. Like, for instance, Christmas gatherings and Thanksgiving also.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It stops, not hardly.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It’s not the same when they leave. That’s the way it was. When my mom was alive at Christmas, like you said, we used to go on Sundays. She would cook and nowadays: nothing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what happens sometimes. It just scatters when that happens.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Sometimes I go to the cemetery and fix all the graves. Me and my daughter go pick up tree limbs and things like that. And we will cut all the grass.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Daylight was my dad’s name in English. Dvyugitsvni was his Cherokee name. He was born when it was turning morning and that’s why they named him Dvyugitsvni. And mom’s name was Ora. Tehee was her last name. Before she turned Owl, Kelvdi was her name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were they born around there, too?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, my dad was born around there, long time ago. They were born in the woods or at home. And my mom was towards Bell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Towards Bell. So, your parents grew up around there where you said they grew up?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, they were together all the time. She would be getting on to me. I would say, “Mom I am an adult.” She would say, “I don’t care. You are still my child. I am your mom and I will get on to you for as long as I live.” “OK,” I would tell her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It really is like that. Like, for instance, your own children, you see them like they are still growing up, as well as your grandchildren and the girl that stays with you.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That girl that stayed with me was over 20, around 24. I told her, “Girl I’m not mad at you. But you’re going to have to grow up and learn when you get by yourself. I am not going to always be alive. You are going to have to learn. I will tell you where to go for help, if you will do it.” We looked for a house, and we found one at Hogner Heights in Stilwell through Cherokee Nation. She was saying, “My dad is mad at me.” I said, “I’m not!” She said, “I’m just saying that.” I told her, “I’m just trying to teach you, ‘cause you have children now and their dad that made them let them go. He is nowhere. We watch them and their grandma. We help them.” I told my daughter, “If you’re not running around drinking, I am going to help you and them kids.” She said, “OK.” and ever since then she has been watching her kids. My mom taught her how to cook. She does everything. She is always cooking and cleaning house. That Pine Sol just lasts her three days. “Dad, I am out of Pine Sol!” I’ll say, “What are you doing? Drinking it?” I’ll say to her. She will say, “I just like cleaning house,” she will say and she really does like cleaning. Them kids always have clean clothes on. I really appreciate her. She is growing up really good. The boy, he is the oldest. I was married to a Seminole for a while. We have two children. She moved away and she found another man and I didn’t know she was pregnant when she left. And that oldest boy didn’t like it and he started to do things that led him to prison. He went in there. They left a long time. I helped him. We used to send money. When my dad was still alive, we used to send money to a lawyer. We got him out the first time. He was in there for almost six years and he got out. I went to visit him. I said, “Boy I am not going to help you, if you mess up, you are going to finish it.” I told him. One time I told all them kids, “I’ll help you all one time. But if you start doing things and you go to jail, you are going to stay in there,” I told him. And he did it again and he went back in, but they gave him a chance after he had been in there a year. “If you finish six months of boot camp, we will let you go,” they told him. So, he asked for boot camp and gangs they have in bigger towns came in there and were crying to get out of that boot camp ‘cause it was really hard, he said. He wanted out, so he lasted six months, and they let him go. They gave him parole and he finished that. He was still living out towards Seminole. He couldn’t find a job because what he done was still following him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What he did, oh yeah.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I went to go get him one time. I went and got him and brought him back and I helped him there in Stilwell where the white people had a program. I helped him there. They gave him a job. It’s been a year since I went and got him and he has been working there ever since. 16 years he has been clean. He is doing real good and he got married and they have their own place, him and that girl. She works in Sallisaw at the dentist. His wife and that boy there in Stilwell. At Swans, he is almost the boss there. They are really doing good. I am thankful for that. I said, “That’s what it took, ain’t it son,” I told him. “Sometimes something like that.” He said, “Yes it did, Dad. I will never go back to it,” he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For some, when they go through something like that, it wakes them up.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yes, it does.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It changes the way they look at things and not the way they did a long time ago. They see it new.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s the way I grew up. I am telling you, when I was young, I used to drink around. I didn’t have anything. I didn’t have a car, and I would pawn stuff and since I have quit, it’s been many years, I can see what I have.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee, man.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I can see, you know. I thank the One above for helping me. He got me out. I should’ve been dead. I have had lots of wrecks. I have thrown cars in the water with me in them. And again He got me through. I still appreciate it. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, like I said, that’s what woke you up.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then, one day He gave you something to think about. He was thinking of you.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what I tell my children.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that is it.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I’m teaching them and hopefully they will teach their kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right, that’s right. Where was it you said you went into the water?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It was towards Nicut. I had never been there before. I don’t know why I went that way. I thought I was going to cross Bradly, but that wasn’t it. I made a wrong turn. I could see the road and I drove in there. That car was sticking out just a little bit. And that one boy was with me, used to be Frank Mink’s oldest son.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It was icy outside – the tree limbs had ice on them. And the water was running. I said, “Walter!” I barely woke him up. He was passed out when that cold water hit him. I told him, “What are we going to do?” He looked around and said, “Where are we at?” I told him, “I don’t know.” He said, “We are going to get out.” So we got out and I tried but he got away from me. I tried, but I was going in the deep. I heard his footsteps. I couldn’t – I was going under. I said, “Walter!” real hard. Again, I swallowed water and came up and said, “Walter!!” again. Later somebody came and pulled me and laid me on that bank. I was this deep. I was laying there. They said he finally made it to someone’s house and then they called people and someone told the highway patrol. They said they looked for me. They said Walter was laying at his house by the stove. They said they barely found me over there. They said he was kicking me, saying, “He’s pretending to be dead.” They said they threw me in his car and told him, “You are taking that other one, too. He is at my house,” he told that highway patrol. And all the people went over there. And when he got to his driveway, he told him, “Now get him out. You ain’t taking him.” That’s how much that guy was helping me that I didn’t know. To this day I don’t know who it is. I just appreciate it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Don’t know who it is.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, I would’ve drowned there if it wasn’t for Walter. It was bad then. When I think about that, I am thankful that He got me through.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, so you are really thankful nowadays.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yes, I am really thankful. Yes really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You went a long ways by the goodness of God. What about when they say your people, clan. What is your people?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They say Long Hair, it’s on my mom’s side, ain’t it? That’s what they used to say.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Anigilo.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: And on my dad’s side, Wolf.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was Wolf. Yeah, what about what you said a while ago. Who was your grandmother? What was her name?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Gane was her name. Lizzie Vann Owl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Lizzie Vann Owl, Gane was her name.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, Gane.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your uncle?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Daniel Owl was his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Daniel Owl.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Daniel Owl was my uncle.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did they grow up?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: There, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just around there.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Around Greasy. There was a road going way out. There was a big house out there, they built. All the children grew up there and he had a garden and an apple tree. It was beautiful. Plums and grapes, different things over here. He was really watching us. I wanted to go pick those apples. He didn’t want us to. He would say, “Haw, Gane! Them kids are on that tree again!"

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They really used to grow stuff like that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, he chose a spot way out in the woods, an open area for his garden. He would be all day with a hoe and pick. I don’t know how long it took him, but he made it pretty big. When it would turn early in the morning, he would go down that way smoking a pipe. He would stay there all day ‘till it was time for him to eat. Them elders didn’t give up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He must’ve had it beautiful.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: He had it beautiful, the dirt grass didn’t even grow. And nowadays, in just a little while, my back starts hurting. “I will get it tomorrow,” I will tell her. That one I have now is a white woman. I will tell her, “I’ll get it tomorrow.” Sometimes I can’t find anyone to talk Cherokee to, and go visit my brother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, it’s a different that white person.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, but she really watches me good. She has been through the same thing. She used to get abused. And still nowadays her ex-husband drinks around. And she knows what it’s like to be mistreated. We have been together for 13 years. She cooks all the time. She will ask if I want something. I will say, “No I am OK.” If I want something she will make it. She washes clothes and cleans the house. I really found a good one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She is doing good for you. What about what you said, your last name Owl. Your last name – you don’t know where it began?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: For a little while I knew. I forget what their names were, the other side I would really like to look. To go back and that, and I want to look. I used to know, but I forgot who it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It started somewhere the last names that we have. Some have worked really hard and had hard and not good times coming along. But nowadays we are going good.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It’s good now, ain’t it? But when those elders were growing up, they used to make ties, and they just used horses to pull them. Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you said, they really worked hard and looking for things in the woods to eat and cook, like for instance.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: There is lots of things out there, still is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, still is.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Some wouldn’t know what to get in the woods. I tell them, “I could live off things in the woods.” Long time ago, mostly salt and grease. We used to kill a hog and we would save the grease and meat we would hang it up and we put salt on it. And say for instance squirrels and rabbits, deer and different things and berries, we would find things like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays young people ain’t like that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They don’t know anything. They will say, “What is that?” if you tell them that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And if you fix a hog and you clean the insides, they will get mad about the smell when it’s cooked.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s good, ain’t it? And with the head, they would make hog head cheese. That’s really good, that meat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and also, I used to really like those pig ears.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Or that part that came from here, ain’t it? That made a broth and they boiled that. I would crumble corn bread.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I remember my dad used to really like those. He used to bite those. It made a sound.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where we lived one time, there was a white man that lived close by. That’s what he used to do. They would bring him hogs and he would fix them. He used to do that and make money. They used to bring a lot. Sometimes he would give me the pigs’ ears, like you said. We knew what we were going to be eating.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: As long as there is beans on.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would bring them every morning to be fixed and he would start early. He would already have water boiling in those big barrels. They would be smoking back, then they would put them in there.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, before they did this.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would pull the table out and put it on there and then with a knife.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Or they would lay a toe sack and then hot water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. They worked really hard back then.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And nowadays they will take them to where they fix them.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, they will do that now. Nobody knows how to fix them or even to castrate the males. We used to raise lots of hogs and chicken. It was really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes on Sundays, did y’all go catch them and do this?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I used to. They still be running around I would have that head – that chicken would still be running really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about what did they used to call you growing up as a boy?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It was Dvyulisni and also they gave me different names at church. Those elders and deacons at church on Sundays, they would cook. There was lots of people, used to be. Jess Vann, used to be Hoolie were brothers. They were in there. I ran over there I said, “Mom! Mom! They were frying chicken!” I said I wanted gatog gatog. That’s when those two named me, “Gatog Hoolie.” That and Jess Rooster and used to be Buck Seabolt, Pedro...Pedro, he would call me. People gave really different names, but that is my real name, Dvyulisni.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I used to know that Buck Seabolt, you’re saying.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: He really was a singer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Aw man, it really made a sound when he sung.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Used to be my uncle, some used to say he was the same way. They had a loud voice. They didn’t need them microphones.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It made a beautiful sound man.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, they used to sing lots of Cherokee songs, a long time ago and now there is a few that sing Cherokee, mostly in English now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There is just a few from a long time ago that used to sing around. It’s running out now. My wife is still able, if she starts. We pastor a church, my wife if she starts a Cherokee song, those that lived long time ago sung, she will start.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But, like we said, we are getting old now.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But, like you said, when someone grows up, it ain’t like that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It’s really not. Some won’t listen to nothing. They will try teach you. My family, I teach them all the time. I rebuke them. I teach them. I even teach them to fix cars. I used to really fix cars when I was able. Them girls will watch more than them boys will.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My wife’s brother used to be married, but his wife is not alive anymore. She was just ye [gesture] tall. Just was his wife, he himself was tall. When their car would break down, she’d get a chair and set it beside the car and that woman would climb up there. She was the one fixing the car. Her husband would be watching from over there. Or if a tire went flat, she could change it fast.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Lots of them can do that, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes people would come, and say, “Can you fix my car?” “Yeah, I can fix it,” he would say, but it would be his wife instead. What about when your parents were alive? Was there something strange they seen where they lived? Anything they talked about most of the time?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, they used to talk about those little people, like that. They had lots of land they had been given, when they came a long time ago. My grandmother had given me some, just by word. “There will be 10 acres if you ever live there.” It was good and flat, it was. The first ones that lived there said they would hear someone talking at night but, no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn’t see anyone?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: No, not until it got dark. They had built the house on their trail. They would come there and go around. They talked about things like that. They saw something when they got to the cemetery. They would go there after dark. Some time we went there at night. My grandmother said her and my grandfather, they took something over. I think it was a lock to fix it. When they got there, something was sitting in a tree. There at the cemetery it was sitting there watching the...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The graves.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, it was human, they said immediately. “We were looking at it. When I opened my door and your grandfather opened his, I looked. It already wasn’t sitting there,” she said. “It was sitting there watching, that something was sitting there on a tree limb high above.” That’s the only thing I have heard about them seeing things. Same thing, I said if they were walking somewhere, they seen something jerking one time. There was a rock ye big... good size rock. We played there and there was lots of tree limbs piled to the side. We were perched. They would walk by ‘cause they walked back sometimes on Sundays while we had a break. And about dark, they would be coming back and they would see something there all the time. Just its feet would be sticking out and it would jerk back like a snake, he was saying. It would go in that pile of something. That was what they talked about and where little people lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There is this one friend of mine, a preacher, where I come from when he was a boy, he said... what do they call lizard in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Teyohali.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Teyohali, different kinds.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That kind. “I never told anyone,” he said “I am just now telling you, we are friends. They would not believe it if I told them.” I thought he said they lived just west of Kenwood on a ridge. There was, like that standing over there, it was wearing a dress and... What do they call it? Bonnet. It was wearing a hat, like that. Its face was like that you said, a lizard, and it had feet like that. “It was looking at me,” he said. I thought, “Boy!” “I looked at it just for a while,” he said. “It was one like that standing over there,” he said. He said he kind of ran. Sometime later there was someone at that store in Kenwood. He was eating there. Someone walked close by and started talking to someone sitting over there and he said there are some people like that living, that white man said. I have seen them too. No one else has ever talked about that. We really are good friends, this preacher. We are almost the same age. I never told anyone, he said I am going to tell you. We were looking around where he grew up when he said. It was standing over there like that. “Boy, I hope one like that don’t come out,” I was thinking. “It was really strange,” he said.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It really was! I mean strange, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It really was, but “I never told anyone because nobody would believe me,” he said.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: And where we used to live, out towards Greasy, Mom and me were sitting one time at night. Around ten, something lived there too. My sister lived just up the hill in a trailer. We were talking. She said, “Levi.” I said, “What?” Mom she said, “Look towards Retha’s house!” Something was on the window. A little person – it was hanging there. It couldn’t reach the [unintelligible]... Just hanging there looking in the house. “It’s those little people,” she said. After a while it jumped down. It was doing this and went into the woods. “Don’t say nothing about it,” Mom said. “You might scare them. Don’t say anything.” But that was the last time we seen it. Yeah, he was hanging on there, just like a small child. He was hanging there looking. His head was doing this.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: That one time, a white man, he was a brick layer. I helped him. He was talking about his aunt, an elder. When they first came where they lived, he was talking about they didn’t have full cabinets. They had curtains. When they got up in the mornings the curtain covers from the bottom would be scattered everywhere. Something would be making noise at night. They really were white people, they were not native. Someone told them to, “Leave food on the table, it will stop.” They did and it did. The noises stopped and what was happening. Yeah, and they were white people, so.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your parents and their parents? For instance, your grandmother’s parents – was there something little they talked about? They heard about Cherokee? Coming from old Cherokee?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They used to tell me. But, like I said, I have forgotten what they told me. Used to be my grandmother would sit all the time. When I got back from school, I would cross straight through the woods. I would go to my grandmother’s. She would cook then I would eat. Then we would sit outside and she would tell me things. But like I said I have forgotten what she has told me. She would tell me what they used to say and the difference from where they came from that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about where you grew up? What was it like where you grew up when you was a boy? When you think back now, was it lots flat land?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It really has changed now from when I was growing up. It was good everywhere, like when they grew peaches and trees, everywhere were pretty. The road was graded. When I go there now the trees are dead. There is nothing planted in them fields. They just have cows in them. It’s really changed good. Lots of people have left. All of the Owls lived over there, was lots of us. The only ones that live there now is Lucille, way up there. And Michael you said lives just this side. That’s the only ones that live there now. Those houses that were there, trees have grown around them. Stuff like that where they lived have grown up. The roads are better now – back then they were dirt roads. They sure needed to be graded. And nowadays...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ... are paved.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Are paved with black top. It’s better and there were stores there. Girdner store was on side of the highway. And when you turned off towards our house, the Asbills had another store. They fixed tires and all. You didn’t have to go Stilwell to get groceries or Sallisaw over there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes when you think about it do you go there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Just when I think about it. Sometimes I want to go there. Sometimes I go across to where I used to live. I will go all the way across, down towards Kentucky. Where there used to be old school, I will turn around and come back towards Starkiller Hollow, they call it, and back across way over there by Sallisaw – that steep hill – I will come out there sometimes. I will turn just this side. In the woods there are turn offs. There are two houses there. You can go across a creek. I haven’t been there in a long time. I don’t know what it’s like now. You can go straight across and come out in Greasy through the woods. I think about things sometimes, how I grew up, where I come from – it was really good long time ago, back then, when I think about it. I have come through here lots of times walking and I look towards the woods where we used to have a trail towards the church and different places that came out towards the road and back towards the woods. We would come out behind the church. People didn’t have lots of cars back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. There lots of you all that lived around there?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Used to be. Long time ago, used to be lots of people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Long time ago. Were the people all Cherokee?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They were all Cherokee. Olie Cantrell was the only white man that lived there and George Limore below the hill and then the Asbills. It started to be white people below the hill and on top all Cherokees.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All Cherokees.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It was, we were friends with all those white people there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all were good there.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, they helped each other out, them people. It was good, I miss it, I tell them sometimes, growing up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you think about it that much sometimes.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, I will sit outside on the porch in the mornings. I pray and be thankful that He got me through. I will talk to Him for a little while, pray for people. When I get done, I just sit there and think about how different it is then where I grew up. Where I live now, I have seen a lot of young people using drugs. I seen a girl one time. There is a railroad track by my house. Her and another boy was walking. The boy crossed, the girl came up and there was a train coming. It was coming fast. She just got in the middle and did this. It was coming right there, close. That boy flew and tackled that girl, and they fell to the ground. Someone seen them from a car that was coming from this way. They got told on, they both got thrown in jail for being drunk and using that stuff – I guess they sniff it. I seen lots of things like that. Boys being on that stuff. They will be fighting among their self and those high line poles that stand there, they will be fighting them and kick those. When they kick them, they will fall down themselves. It is bad where I live, by my house you can see lots of things. When I think back man it was not like that where I used to live. I was living good. It was peaceful and quiet everything everybody knew everybody. It was really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: An also you all played good.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Marbles – we would have holes here. Mom would be getting on to us. We had dirty clothes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You think I should have kept those? They buy them at the store nowadays. They pay a lot for pants with lots of holes.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Again, me and the boys would play cowboys and Indians, in the woods. We pretended sticks to be guns. We would go everywhere in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all ran around.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I miss that. I tell the girls sometimes what I did in the past, I mean I made bad decisions when I grew up, but I corrected them. I tell them by the grace of God I am still going.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was good.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s what my dad used to tell me. Like I am saying, my dad was a deacon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about over time, when they cooked something to eat, what did you like? From a long time ago that they made and cooked?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Beans, hog meat, gravy, and potatoes – that and corn bread patties some used to make. I would eat – I could not get enough beans.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Corn dodgers you said.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Corn bread, they used to make biscuits with corn meal with hot warm water. They would do this. They were good. Even snacks, if we were hungry around midnight around 10, Mom would get up and make those with salt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, me too, my wife sometimes makes those. Like that if there is some left over, she will say, “Someone might eat these. When you wake up in the morning, they would not on the side be there.”

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really was; she was a good cook. They would have beans in those they called warmers with wood. Them beans were really good with wood, if you put them on there all day.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I remember when I was a boy, I used to get tired of food like that, but now I would really want that.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: You will miss that. I still eat things like that. That old woman will make that for me all the time. I have not ate onion yet, but yesterday evening I found some. My ex-wife brought me some. Nowadays we get along good, my ex-wife. It’s better, I think. Maybe it was meant to be that we get along better nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good, that’s good. It’s good there is no hatred involved.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: It really is. Nothing can be done about it – just happened. That’s why we all still work together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Someone that goes to church gave us onion. My wife said, “I am going to cook beans.” Yeah, that kind we are talking about made of corn bread. Boy, man we ate good.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I am getting hungry now.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Me too!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you said, I was splashing grease and salt beans the same.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That grease after you kill a hog – that is good grease. It gives it that flavor for beans. I smash them beans and put grease and then more grease.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then I smash them up with a fork. I do this, then grease and salt. What about... toward the last – does Cherokee have a different sound when the new learners talk? For instance, the learners here? And how you talked in Cherokee growing up?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Yeah, there is little difference. I don’t know how they do it. I mean, I understand what they are talking about. It is a little different. Sometimes I listen to them on the phone. “This is my name. This is what I am going to teach you to say today.” I know what they are talking about, but they say it a little different then when I was growing up. They think the same way about Cherokees that come from a different place, like North Carolina, when we hear it. I was going to tell you, Kentucky, I think it was, I was working. They came from Toward the Rising Sun, Michelle Hicks is the chief’s name.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, was.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: His wife and a white woman were in Kentucky. We were working in an open store. We were remodeling it and everything. We were blocking it off and me and Emit Gonzalis used to be were sitting there fixing. Some women came over there and stood – they were looking for something. Me and Emit were talking in Cherokee. That woman did this and was looking at us. I was wondering why she kept looking at us. Emit was saying, “Ask them what they want.” I told him, “No, they might beat me up!” That was her, the chief’s wife and that other one. She also had a crew that was hers, then they moved. Then I went looking for something in the truck. I went to get out a battery or something. When I went out, they were standing outside them. They said, “Sir.” “Are you talking to me?” I told them. They said yes. I said, “What can I do for you?” “We heard you talking in Cherokee in there,” they said. “That was Cherokee.” “Yes, ma’am,” I said. “We know you are not from this side, North Carolina, because it is a little different,” they said. “No, I am from towards Stilwell, towards Tahlequah, Cherokee Nation down,” I told her. She said, “We thought so! We heard you talking in there and I told her.” She said her name. “You got be from there,” she said. Then we talked for a little while. They said, “Can we talk to you?” “When I get a break. In about 30 more minutes, I will be getting a break, but yeah,” I told them. I went back in. When we got a break, they were sitting there. I walked over there and we talked. “How many of you all are Cherokees?” she said. “Probably about four of us.” They asked what we did. I said we travel anywhere from Texas, California, Kentucky, West Virginia. I told her, “Pennsylvania and Colorado remodeling and building new stores,” I told her. “Ok, how long you all got here?” she said. “Probably about two more weeks,” I told her. “We will make sure we come back and see you in about a week,” they said. “Well it was nice meeting you,” and we shook hands and that weekend we came home they gave us a few days off – not a few days. We would leave there on a Friday evening, we would get back Saturday morning. Sunday afternoon we would be going again. When we got back to our work, they were there. “When are you going to go eat?” “About 12,” I told them. They said, “We are going to buy you lunch or whatever you call it. We are going to buy it. There is a café over there,” they said. “We will drive you down there and take you over there,” they said. “You are not kidnapping me are you?” I told them. “No, no! We just need to talk to you.” “OK.” So I told the boss. He said, “We were going over there and eat, to kind of keep an eye on you.” “It’s the chief’s wife,” I told them. So we talked there. And my sister’s husband, a white man, Dave, he was sitting there behind me. They offered me a job. We talked for a little while. That woman said, “Where are you all staying?” I told her. “Do you all across that big river? Across that big bridge?” she said. I said yes. “Do you all ever see them buildings, them two buildings?” she said. I said, “Yeah.” “Them red ones – those are mine. They are my offices,” she said. “I will talk to her and talk to Michelle Hicks. If you want, you can work for me,” she said. “You can take from Arkansas to back this way. Texas – that’s how far we go and I will keep the boys off this, all this way. If you take it, we will buy you a brand new truck,” she said. “That Michelle and his wife and all of that, we will buy it, Levi,” she said. “We will buy you a trailer. We will buy all the tools you need,” they told me. “And how many boys would you need?” “If I did work I usually do, I would use five or six, ‘cause that’s how many I had here to get things done,” I told her. “That would too many for one truck. We will buy you another one, but it won’t be a brand new one but a used one, but up to date,” she said. “If you want to do it that way and if you ever quit, that stuff is yours,” they said for some reason. I didn’t take it. That one, my brother-in-law, when we came back, “Why didn’t you just take it? I will be your lead man. I will be your right hand.” And then, “I am sorry I can’t because you don’t know what you are doing,” I told him. Yeah, I had opportunities. Texas too I had opportunity over there but didn’t take it. That would take me away too long from my family, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For instance nowadays they are learning in Cherokee here. What do you think about it, 20 years or 10 years, if we are still living or it gets there this school here, what do you think? Do you think the Cherokee language will still be here?

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: If we continue to teach the children, it will still be here but it is up to us all to do that, to teach them and to keep it going to teach them. And when you all grow up, keep going. Keep teaching children. If it’s like that, it will get that far still yet. That’s to be talking but if they don’t care if children don’t want learn, it’s just going to go somewhere. And there is too many, mixed racial, getting together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Have Mexican children.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Mexican and Whites different kinds, that’s what happens nowadays. If it happens like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It will be going down.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That is what is happening nowadays. You know, it would be good if it is alive in 20 years, but it is up to us grownups to care to teach them and them to teach others. And if they learn, it is good that they are learning. If we can get these kids to come.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really what they are doing, teaching Cherokee, we need to help the teachers.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We can work together with the teachers. Maybe they will learn more, but not just some bring them here, so the teachers can teach them. Their parents some don’t speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: They don’t. They should try. They should come here and sit down with them, all of them. We are going to have to help each other. Like you said, we have to help these teachers with that. Give them confidence in doing it. We got to help them out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That is the way they learn. I was reading, for instance if a baby is born if the parents talk all Cherokee, if they talk all Cherokee, they talk to it in Cherokee and when they do talk to it in Cherokee, it looks into their eyes. And when we talk to them in Cherokee, we need to look into its eyes. When we are talking in Cherokee something happens in its brain, they are going to learn what it is. It gets hard then.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: That’s what they used to say. My dad used to say that, “Talk to them kids in Cherokee,” and that’s what I did, talk to them in Cherokee but that Seminole would talk in English. But I would say, “Hey, I am talking to them in Cherokee!?” I would talk to them in Cherokee. Like I said, that one grandchild, I was telling her. When I was fixing cars, she would come. She is about six maybe seven years old and say, “Papa, how do you say this?” She would point at a tree and a dog, car, house and a door, window – different things she would ask. She would do that, then one day she started getting those milk crates for chairs and say, “Time for school Papa!” She would sit down. I would teach her something simple to say. I would teach her like that she can still do it. But talking, she can understand a little bit now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good now in English communicate saying now their eyes she looks at their eyes and they look at her eyes.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: Really, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I appreciate it, appreciate it.

segments.speaker: levi-owl
segments.translation: I really appreciate it too. We talked that long. I think I am losing my Cherokee now, like I said, we talk English all the time.
